headline: High: A’s broad networked CRM/email surfaces plus B’s shell/MCP/git capabilities create dangerous default pathways for leakage, prompt injection, and destructive downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can ingest CRM, email, Slack, Notion, and Google Sheets content, while B can use MCP/stdin-stdout and background workers. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if A’s outputs are fed into B without sanitization. The interaction is inferred from docs, not directly observed, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF A outputs are forwarded into B's MCP/stdin pipeline without provenance filtering, injection is possible.
IF shared workspace content is parsed as instructions by B, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding from A to B.
Strip instructions from A-originated text before B reads it.
Add a provenance tag to every A output.
Review B prompts for instruction-following on untrusted text.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization middleware between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches CRM, customer support, email, and calendar data and has broad network egress; B can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, use MCP, and modify git state. Even without a shared filesystem explicitly documented, the pair can move sensitive A data into B’s outbound channels or logs. Because the bridge is inferred and not directly documented, I choose high over medium due to the sensitive data classes and egress risk.
conditions: IF A data is passed to B through MCP, shell, or git artifacts, sensitive CRM/email/calendar content can leak.
IF B logs or commits A-originated content, that content may persist outside intended retention.
mitigations: Block sensitive fields before handoff to B.
Turn off B network egress for A-derived tasks.
Use a separate workspace for A and B.
Audit B logs for A-originated secrets.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on inter-agent transfers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress and multiple-instance support; B can write shell, install packages, modify git state, and use MCP. Their write surfaces overlap on mutable external resources and repositories, so concurrent actions can conflict even if no shared directory is documented. Uncertainty about the exact shared target keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or remote resource, race conditions can corrupt state.
IF A and B run concurrently without locking, one agent can overwrite the other's changes.
mitigations: Serialize writes to shared resources.
Assign separate branches or workspaces.
Pause one agent during the other's write phase.
Add a lock file or lease before mutation.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate CRM/email/calendar actions and B can execute shell, modify git state, and dispatch background tasks. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into irreversible commits or external actions. The pairwise pathway is inferred from docs, but the downstream authority makes the blast radius high.
conditions: IF B consumes A outputs without verification, incorrect facts can trigger wrong actions.
IF A-generated content is used to drive B's shell or git operations, mistakes can become persistent.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A outputs.
Add a verification step between agents.
Limit B to read-only mode for A-derived tasks.
Log and diff all A-to-B handoffs.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for A outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles CRM, customer support, email, and calendar data, while B handles code, repository metadata, and task prompts. The profiles do not document residency or certification mismatches, so I cannot claim a specific breach. However, the mixed data classes and B’s outbound-capable tooling create a plausible retention/logging mismatch, which is enough for medium under uncertainty.
conditions: IF regulated customer data from A is routed into B's logs or repositories, retention obligations may be violated.
IF A data crosses jurisdictions through B's network egress, residency controls may fail.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B inputs.
Redact personal data before transfer.
Set short log retention on both agents.
Review jurisdictional routing for outbound calls.
requires-engineering: add policy-based data classification gates.
